parts: ORIGINS OF THE BREED

Although its proper name is the Old English Sheepdog, it is known throughout the world as the Bobtail, from the English words "bob", meaning cut short, and "tail". This name dates back to the 16th century, when a law was passed exempting all working animals, whether dogs, horses or others, from tax. Their tails were docked as a distinguishing mark, allowing them to be identified more quickly when taxes were collected. These dogs became popularly known as "Bobtailied Dogs", meaning dogs with docked tails.

Some nobles and wealthy people docked their hunting dogs' tails simply to save a few pennies. This prompted the introduction of a new law in 1776 allowing working dogs to keep their tails. The law was revised again in 1878, making it clear that docking was unnecessary.

A law in force in the United Kingdom since 1959, and revised in 1969, also exempts working animals from tax. Hunting is considered a sport, however, so hunting dogs are subject to the required fees. The docking tradition has survived to the present day, even though the old law is no longer in force. Indeed, breed standards implicitly require the tail to be docked at the first caudal vertebra between the 2nd and 8th day after birth, leaving a tail approximately one centimetre long in adulthood.

Another theory holds that docking served a practical purpose, as the tail could get in the way while the dog worked and, in a fight with a wolf, offered the predator an easy grip. Whatever the original reasons may have been, docking continues to be practised. Another explanation for the tradition in this breed is that many shepherds believed dogs would be less agile without their tails, which help them balance as they move and act as a rudder. The breed's founders did not want a fast, agile dog that might exhaust the sheep. Instead, they preferred a dog that would guide the flock at a slower, steadier pace.
Today, this custom is still observed for aesthetic reasons and has remained unchanged since the first breed club was established in 1888.

This dog, admired for its striking appearance and temperament, has not performed the work for which it was bred for many years. Nevertheless, it was an excellent drover, not only of sheep but also, as records show, of cattle, particularly on the journeys from the pastures to Smithfield, home to one of the most famous livestock markets.

The Bobtail has considerable ability as a sheepdog, although its appearance gives little indication of its remarkable working capabilities. It could still be seen tending sheep at the beginning of the century, before becoming, in later years, a member of the family that so lovingly pampers it and cares for its appearance.

The Bobtail's shaggy appearance conveys a ruggedness that it genuinely possesses, while also creating the misleading impression of a very ancient breed. In fact, the Bobtail as we know it today has no more than 200 years of scientifically verifiable history.

Its distinctive appearance and rather bold, mischievous temperament have made it popular among dog enthusiasts. It has appeared in numerous films, including "Chitty chitty bang bang" and Walt Disney films that gave it a starring role, such as "Un candidato muy peludo", "Una vida de perros" and "La Sirenita", as well as in advertisements and several animated series.
HISTORY

As for its origins, its resemblance to the Briard and the Italian Bergamasco, and consequently to the Russian Owtcharka, suggests that they share common ancestry. Some authors maintain that during the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453), several Briards were introduced into Scotland, where they developed along a parallel but somewhat different path from the French sheepdog. This would place their origins in the Scottish Highlands. The English dispute this, however, claiming that the breed originated around the county of Devon, which lies only a short distance from France, and that its ancestors include the Water Dog and the Derhound.

In any case, two things are clear: neither of these two dogs has the Bobtail's expression and intelligent gaze, and there is a certain resemblance between the Bobtail and the Scottish Bearded Collie, although the latter is somewhat longer in body, while the Bobtail is sturdier and squarer.

Some people, noting the Bobtail's bear-like gait, a resemblance heightened by its distinctive appearance, have suggested that bears must somehow have contributed to the breed. This alone should give readers an idea of the credibility of some supposedly expert theories.
Some writers attribute the breed to Scotland, and more specifically to the Highlands.

In our view, this is another example of the pattern seen in the origins of almost all sheepdogs: one does not descend from another; rather, they all share common ancestry. Each breed developed under a range of influences, including its region, terrain, climate and suitability for particular work. Crossbreeding with local dogs must also be taken into account.

In 1883, Aidstone described a type of sheepdog working in Oxford, Wiltshire, Berkshire, Hampshire, Somerset and Dorset that was very probably a Bobtail. He described it as: "Blue, grizzled, harsh-coated, long-legged, rugged, with small eyes and ears, and no tail...". In modern times, the most widely accepted theory rejects a Scottish origin, holding instead that the breed is native to the lowland regions of England.
The breed can be considered to have become established in its present form during the 19th century. An oil painting by Lilian Cheviot from 1910 depicts a dog just as we know the breed today.

Its show-ring history began in 1863, when two dogs were entered for the first time in the English Sheepdogs category at "The First International Dogschow" in Islington. The winner was a handsome male named Rover, owned by Mr. W. Grummit. He was sold to Mr. t. Wootton and took 2nd place at the Birmingham show later that year. The finest dog of that period was a male of the same name who achieved excellent results: 2nd at Cremorne in 1864, 1st at Islington in 1864-1865, and 1st at Manchester in 1865 and 1867.

The breed's success was clear, and in 1873 the first dog was registered in the Kennel Club Stud Book (K.C.S.B.). That same year, three dogs were shown at Curzon Hall in Birmingham, entered as English Short-Tailed Sheepdogs. They were judged by Mr. M. Wynn, who, revealing his limited knowledge of the breed, awarded only 2nd place to Ben, owned by Mr. J. Smith, and withheld 1st place.

After this show, disaster seemed to loom over the Bobtail's early development. In 1889, however, Mr. Freeman Lloy produced an explanatory pamphlet about the breed that greatly supported the selective breeding work being undertaken by the Old English Sheepdog Club.

One of the club's presidents, Mrs. Fare Fosse, owned a female named Fairweather who became an English Champion. This exceptional dog was so beautiful that, after her death, she was preserved by taxidermy as an ideal example of the breed. She can now be seen at the Natural History Museum in Trigh.

The breed's history over the past 100 years owes much to the Tilley family, whose work has passed from one generation to the next throughout that time. Their kennel, named Sheptom, continues to exist today thanks to Mrs. Florence Tilley.
THE BOBTAIL ARRIVES IN AMERICA

Records show that the first Bobtail imported into the United States was "Bob", purchased by G. Kennels of Pennsylvania in 1885. By 1890, five years after its arrival, the breed had already taken 2nd place at the "Westminster Kennel Club Show" in New York. This important dog show is now held annually at Madison Square Garden in New York. As many as 56 Bobtails competed at that Westminster Kennel event, showing that the breed was beginning to gain popularity among American breeders. The American Kennel Club had officially recognised the Bobtail as a breed two years earlier, in 1888. This demonstrates the breeders' commitment to securing full recognition for the breed.

Since then, the number of pedigree Bobtails registered with the American Kennel Club has continued to rise. Today, many respected breeders across the country produce healthy, strong and very attractive dogs. The Bobtail is now also kept as a family pet and show dog, participates to some extent in obedience trials and, in smaller numbers, still works on farms and ranches.
The breed club was founded in the USA in 1904 and quickly spread across the states.
Mr. Henry A. Tilley founded the club, crossing the Atlantic to establish the Old English Sheepdog of America, which had only 10 members at its inception.
THE BOBTAIL ARRIVES IN SPAIN

The breed first appeared in Spain around 1969-1970, with Lameda Mistic Lady (no. 27203) among the pioneers. Imported dogs, mainly from England, formed the foundation of breeding. Early kennel names dedicated to the breed included "El Escorial", "Xamahibar" and "Pambre".
